name: Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Heart Rhythm Society Expert Consensus Statement 2015

criteria.description: Sustained heart rate increase of >=30 bpm (or >=40 bpm in adolescents 12-19) within 10 minutes of standing or head-up tilt, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension (BP drop >20/10 mmHg)
Symptoms of orthostatic intolerance present for at least 3-6 months
Absence of other conditions that could explain tachycardia (dehydration, medications, prolonged bed rest, anemia, thyroid dysfunction)
Standing heart rate frequently exceeds 120 bpm
Symptoms worsen with standing and improve with recumbency

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All three major criteria must be met
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Head-up tilt table test or active standing test is the standard diagnostic method. 24-hour Holter monitoring may support diagnosis.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Excessive heart rate increase on standing (>=30 bpm)

occasional.notes: Purplish discoloration of lower legs on standing

laboratory: Elevated standing norepinephrine (>600 pg/mL in hyperadrenergic subtype)
Low blood volume on DAXOR blood volume testing
imaging: QSART may show abnormal sweat responses
Thermoregulatory sweat test abnormalities in neuropathic subtype
genetic: NET gene (SLC6A2) mutations in rare familial cases
other: Head-up tilt table test: HR increase >=30 bpm within 10 min
Active standing test with continuous HR/BP monitoring
Valsalva maneuver may show abnormal blood pressure responses

distinguishingFeatures: IST has elevated resting heart rate (>100 bpm) not just on standing
IST lacks the marked orthostatic HR increment seen in POTS
NCS features bradycardia and hypotension at the time of syncope
POTS features tachycardia without significant blood pressure drop
Neurogenic OH has a sustained BP drop >20/10 mmHg on standing
POTS does not have sustained orthostatic hypotension
MCAS may cause flushing and tachycardia but has elevated tryptase during episodes

redFlags: Rapidly progressive autonomic symptoms suggesting autoimmune or paraneoplastic cause
New onset after viral illness may suggest post-infectious autoimmune etiology
Weight loss or night sweats suggesting malignancy
references: Sheldon RS, et al. 2015 Heart Rhythm Society Expert Consensus Statement on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Postural Tachycardia Syndrome. Heart Rhythm. 2015;12(6):e41-e63.

Vernino S, et al. Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS): State of the Science and Clinical Care from a 2019 National Institutes of Health Expert Consensus Meeting. Auton Neurosci. 2021;235:102828.
Raj SR, et al. Long-COVID postural tachycardia syndrome: an American Autonomic Society statement. Clin Auton Res. 2021;31(3):365-368.
